summary: A 1933 pole tower on the Idaho line was replaced in 1953 by the 40-ft tower standing today, which is staffed in summer.

facts.design: L-4 live-in cab on a 40-ft treated timber tower (1953); first tower was a 30-ft L-4 pole tower (1933)

access.note: On Forest Service land. The road is usually open to within about a mile of the summit from July 1 to Labor Day and is often gated near 4,200 ft at other times. Sources do not say whether visitors may enter the cab.

visit.trail_note: Gate near 4,200 ft often closed outside July 1 to Labor Day: 3.3 mi round trip, 860 ft gain. Gate open: about 1.5 mi round trip on an old ridge trail (TrailChick, 2018 visit).

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service (Priest Lake Ranger District, Idaho Panhandle National Forest)

events.note: First tower on the site: 30-ft L-4 pole tower
Replaced by the present 40-ft treated timber tower with 14x14-ft L-4 live-in cab

evidence.quote: County: Pend Oreille Land: Idaho Panhandle National Forest

evidence.supports: administered by Priest Lake Ranger District; just inside Washington
evidence.quote: Administered by the Priest Lake Ranger District, the lookout is located just west of the state line in Washington.

evidence.supports: quarter mile inside Washington from Idaho border
evidence.quote: Indian Mtn. is a scant 1/4 mile inside Washington from the Idaho border.

evidence.supports: 1933 30-ft pole L-4 tower; 1953 replacement 40-ft timber tower with L-4 cab
evidence.quote: A 30' pole L-4 tower was constructed in 1933, replaced by the present 40' treated timber tower with L-4 cab in 1953.

evidence.supports: 1953 40-ft tower with 14x14 L-4 live-in cab and catwalk
evidence.quote: The current 40’ wooden tower (the second on the site) was built in 1953 and supports a 14’ x 14’ L-4 live-in cab with catwalk.
The site was established in 1933 with a 30' L-4 tower, then replaced in 1953 with the present 40' treated timber tower with L-4 cab.
Indian Mountain Lookout has been staffed every season since the first tower was constructed in 1933.

evidence.supports: regularly staffed during summer fire seasons (2014 photo entry)
evidence.quote: The tower is regularly staffed during Summer fire seasons.

evidence.supports: Kaniksu forest had over a dozen lookouts; Indian Mountain ranked first for initial detection
evidence.quote: When the Kaniksu National Forest had over a dozen active lookouts, Indian Mountain was ranked first for initial detection reports.

evidence.supports: Kaniksu and Idaho Panhandle names for the same forest

evidence.quote: The lookout is staffed in the summer and is on the National Historic Lookout Register

evidence.supports: drive to within a mile of summit in summer, then ridge trail
evidence.quote: From July 1 through Labor Day you can usually drive to within a mile of Indian's summit, then hike a short ridge trail up.

evidence.supports: road often gated around 4,200 ft to protect huckleberries and wildlife habitat
evidence.quote: the road is often gated around 4,200' to help maintain huckleberries and wildlife habitat

evidence.supports: 3.3 mile round trip, 860 ft gain when gated
evidence.quote: If the road is gated at 4,200', Indian is a 3.3 mile round trip hike gaining 860'.

evidence.supports: ridge hike for views of Priest Lake
evidence.quote: Beautiful views of Priest Lake. Hiking the ridge trail/singletrack.

corrections.why: 9.1 m equals 30 ft, the height of the 1933 pole tower. The standing tower was built in 1953 at 40 ft, about 12.2 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1933 is the first tower on the site and 1953 is the current 40-ft tower. The two years describe different structures on one site, so both are correct.

notes_for_editor: Record height 9.1 m is the 1933 tower (30 ft); the standing 40-ft tower is about 12.2 m. Staffing as_of 2024 is the date of TrailChick's last update, not a dated staffing report; NHLR's every-season claim is undated. Do not merge with the Idaho lookout also named Indian Mountain (nhlr.org/lookouts/us/id/indian-mountain-lookout/, Payette NF, a different structure) that appeared in search results. No notable fires were found in the sources read. Access 'public' reflects Forest Service land and a seasonal road gate; no source on cab entry was read.
